records.clean_question: The 1994 national mean daily hospital cost was USD 931. A random sample of 30 Massachusetts hospital costs has mean USD 1,131. Assume $\sigma=333$ dollars. Test at $\alpha=0.05$ whether the Massachusetts mean exceeded USD 931.
records.clean_answer: Test $H_0:\mu=931$ versus $H_a:\mu>931$. The statistic is $z=(1131-931)/(333/\sqrt{30})\approx3.29$, with one-sided p-value about $0.0005$. Reject $H_0$; there is sufficient evidence that the Massachusetts mean exceeded USD 931.

records.clean_question:
In 1990, mean annual passenger-vehicle mileage was 10.3 thousand miles. A random sample of 500 vehicles has mean 10.1 thousand miles; assume known $\sigma=6.0$ thousand miles.

a. Test $H_0:\mu=10.3$ versus $H_a:\mu\ne10.3$ at $\alpha=0.05$.

b. Construct a 95% confidence interval for $\mu$.
records.clean_answer:
a. $z=(10.1-10.3)/(6/\sqrt{500})\approx-0.745$, so the two-sided p-value is about 0.456. Fail to reject $H_0$.

b. The 95% interval is $10.1\pm1.96(6/\sqrt{500})=[9.574,10.626]$ thousand miles.

records.clean_question:
A shipment may contain at most 2% defective electric can openers. In a random sample of 400, 11 are defective.

a. Test at $\alpha=0.05$ whether the defect rate exceeds 2%.

b. Report and interpret the observed significance level.
records.clean_answer: Let $H_0:p=0.02$ versus $H_a:p>0.02$. Here $\hat p=11/400=0.0275$ and $\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.02(0.98)/400}=0.007$. Thus $z=(0.0275-0.02)/0.007=1.07$, with p-value about 0.142. Fail to reject $H_0$ at 0.05; the observed result is not sufficiently unusual to conclude that the defect rate exceeds 2%.

records.clean_question:
Miranda samples 60 people from Adam's House at Harvard and finds 44 with piercings.

a. Test $H_0:p\le0.60$ versus $H_a:p>0.60$ at $\alpha=0.05$.

b. Identify a sampling concern.
records.clean_answer:
a. $\hat p=44/60=0.7333$. Under $p_0=0.60$, $\operatorname{SE}=\sqrt{0.6(0.4)/60}=0.06325$, so $z=(0.7333-0.60)/0.06325=2.11$ and p-value $\approx0.0175$. Reject $H_0$; the sample supports a proportion above 60%.

b. Adam's House is a convenience sample, not a random sample of all Harvard students, so the result may suffer selection bias and cannot be generalized reliably.

records.clean_question: In a blind taste test, 56 of 100 Diet Coke drinkers prefer Diet Pepsi. Test $H_0:p=0.50$ versus $H_a:p>0.50$ at $\alpha=0.05$, and state the consequence for the advertising claim.
records.clean_answer: $\hat p=0.56$, $\operatorname{SE}_0=0.05$, and $z=(0.56-0.50)/0.05=1.20$. The p-value is 0.1151, so fail to reject $H_0$. The sample does not provide sufficient evidence that more than half prefer Diet Pepsi; the claim is not statistically supported.

records.clean_question: Historically, 37% of cars failed a pollution standard. In a recent sample of 100 cars, 28% failed. Test at $\alpha=0.01$ whether cars have improved (a lower failure rate). State hypotheses in words and symbols, compute the statistic and p-value, and interpret the conclusion.
records.clean_answer: Let $H_0:p=0.37$ (the failure rate has not improved) and $H_a:p<0.37$ (the failure rate is lower). The statistic is $z=(0.28-0.37)/\sqrt{0.37(0.63)/100}\approx-1.86$, with p-value about 0.031. Since 0.031>0.01, fail to reject $H_0$; at the 1% level there is insufficient evidence that the failure rate improved.

records.clean_question: A sample of 50 regular-coffee drinkers has mean 4.35 cups/day and $s=1.20$; a sample of 40 decaffeinated-coffee drinkers has mean 5.84 cups/day and $s=1.36$. Assuming independent populations, test at $\alpha=0.01$ whether regular drinkers consume less and report the p-value.

The one-sided p-value is $2.9\times10^{-7}$, so reject $H_0$; regular-coffee drinkers consume less on average.
